strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: efficiently adapting LoRA to a wide range of quantization configurations for heterogeneous edge devices without repeated fine-tuning.

The core idea of a lightweight configuration-aware hypernetwork that outputs compact r x r adjustment matrices (rather than mapping to the full LoRA parameter space) is a reasonable and efficient design choice, motivated by an empirical observation (Appendix C.1) that adaptation signal concentrates in L2.

The Pareto/GP-based configuration search with finite-difference guided optimization and diversity-preserving segmented filtering is a sensible approach to the otherwise intractable problem of selecting a good training configuration set in a huge discrete space.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation: multiple GLUE tasks, three LLM backbones from 1.5B to 7B, perplexity on C4, zero-shot downstream evaluation, and ablations on rank, number of segments, and configuration search effectiveness.
Demonstrates favorable trade-off of time cost vs. accuracy relative to one-to-one fine-tuning baselines (Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA), and shows reasonable generalization to unseen configurations.
weaknesses: The HV-based comparison between CoA-LoRA (evaluated at 50 configurations) and baselines (evaluated only at 4 bit-widths due to cost) is not entirely apples-to-apples; it is unclear whether the reported HV/accuracy gains would hold if baselines were evaluated on a comparable spread of configurations, or whether the comparison partly exploits the differing evaluation granularity.

Missing comparisons to other potentially relevant dynamic/switchable or once-for-all-style adapters or quantization-aware PEFT methods beyond Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA/Shared-LoRA/GPTQ-LoRA, leaving open whether CoA-LoRA is compared against the true state of the art for elastic/configurable fine-tuning.

Task scope is fairly narrow: primarily GLUE classification tasks and language-model perplexity/zero-shot QA; no generation-quality or instruction-following evaluation, which is increasingly standard for LLM fine-tuning papers.

Limited transparency on the size/overhead of the configuration-aware model θ itself (parameter count, architecture details, added inference/training overhead), and the cost of the Pareto/GP configuration search (calibration passes, GP fitting, MIP solves) is not clearly separated from the reported total training time.

No reported variance/error bars across multiple runs or seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported accuracy gains, some of which are relatively small (e.g., <1% in several cells of Table 3).

The initial configuration set construction relies on solving a mixed-integer program (via Gurobi) per configuration; scalability of this step to larger models with many more layers/blocks is not analyzed.

Some claims (e.g., 'no additional time cost') are strong relative to the evidence, since the method still requires nontrivial one-time training and search overhead that is not fully decomposed or compared against the cumulative cost of baselines at a matched number of configurations.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: enabling a single fine-tuned adapter to serve heterogeneous quantization configurations across edge devices, avoiding the linear scaling cost of per-configuration LoRA fine-tuning.

The idea of factorizing the mapping to only adjust L2 via a lightweight r×r matrix (based on the empirical observation that quantization-specific information concentrates in L2) is a reasonable design choice that keeps the configuration-aware model compact.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple model sizes (RoBERTa-Large, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B), multiple task types (GLUE classification, C4 language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks), and several ablations (rank, number of Pareto segments, presence/absence of configuration search).
Reports concrete time savings compared to per-configuration fine-tuning baselines (Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA), which is a relevant practical metric for the motivating use case.
weaknesses: The headline hypervolume (HV) comparisons are not apples-to-apples: CoA-LoRA is evaluated on 50 configurations spanning 2.5–6.25 bits, whereas Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA are only evaluated at 4 discrete bit-widths (2.5, 3, 3.5, 4 bits) due to cost. Since HV integrates over a wider objective space when more points/higher bit-widths are included, CoA-LoRA's HV advantage may largely reflect this broader coverage rather than genuinely stronger per-point performance, which the paper does not disentangle.

The paper's own tables partially contradict its central claim of consistent superiority: e.g., in Table 3 at r=64, CoA-LoRA's accuracy gap on MNLI is -0.63% while LQ-LoRA achieves +2.73%; LQ-LoRA outperforms CoA-LoRA in several rank/task combinations. The abstract/conclusion's framing ('comparable or superior', gains up to 10.37%) overstates the consistency of the results.

QA-LoRA (Xu et al., 2024), a directly relevant quantization-aware LoRA method cited in related work, is never used as an experimental baseline despite being arguably the closest prior method to this paper's problem setting.

The finite-difference gradient approximation over learned, jointly-optimized layer embeddings (Eq. 7-8) is presented with minimal justification or analysis; it is unclear why treating a moving, learned embedding space with unit-step finite differences constitutes a meaningful or stable gradient signal for a discrete configuration space, and no convergence or sensitivity study for this component is given beyond varying the number of Pareto segments U.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided anywhere in the paper; all reported accuracy gains (2.36%–10.37%) and HV numbers are single-run point estimates, which is insufficient to support claims of consistent, significant improvement over baselines.

The method is tightly coupled to the NormalFloat (NF) quantization scheme and its specific five-parameter layer configuration; generalization to other widely-used quantization schemes (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ) is only lightly touched via a GPTQ-LoRA baseline comparison and not integrated into the core configuration-aware framework, limiting the claimed generality of 'arbitrary quantization configurations.'

The initial configuration-set construction (Appendix A.1) relies on solving a mixed 0-1 integer program per configuration via a commercial solver (Gurobi), adding a non-trivial and somewhat externally dependent component to the pipeline whose cost/impact on reproducibility is not fully discussed.

The scalability claims in Observation 2 are supported only by qualitative visual comparison of curves (Fig. 6) without a corresponding quantitative HV/gap table analogous to Table 2, making it hard to verify how the benefits scale (or shrink) with model size.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: enabling a single LoRA adapter to generalize across heterogeneous, arbitrary quantization configurations without repeated per-configuration fine-tuning, which is important for edge deployment scenarios.

The design is motivated by an empirical observation (Appendix C.1) that configuration-specific adaptation signal concentrates in L1 while L2 carries shared knowledge, which justifies the lightweight r x r adjustment matrix design and meaningfully reduces the output dimensionality of the configuration-aware mapping.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning multiple model scales (RoBERTa-Large, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B), multiple task types (GLUE classification, C4 language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks), and multiple baselines (Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA, Shared-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA).

Includes several informative ablations: effect of configuration search (Fig. 8), sensitivity to rank (Table 3), sensitivity to number of Pareto segments U (Fig. C.2), and generalization to unseen configurations (Fig. 7/A.1), which help substantiate design choices.
Reports both accuracy/perplexity and wall-clock training time, directly addressing the practical trade-off the paper claims to solve.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—conditioning a hypernetwork-like mapping on a task configuration to produce low-rank adjustments—is conceptually close to existing hypernetwork/conditional-adapter ideas; the novelty is mainly in applying this to quantization configurations rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The finite-difference gradient approximation (Eq. 7-8) operates on continuous learned embeddings Ci, but actual evaluation of f1(C) requires quantizing weights with discrete parameters (b0, b1, b2, B0, B1); the paper does not clearly explain how perturbed continuous embeddings are mapped back to valid discrete quantization configurations for evaluation, leaving a significant methodological gap in reproducibility and correctness.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the paper, despite many reported gains being in the 0.5%-2% range (e.g., Table 3 accuracy gaps), which makes it hard to assess whether the claimed superiority over Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA is robust or within noise.

The comparison in Table 2/Fig. 5 evaluates CoA-LoRA over 50 configurations but baselines (Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA) only at 4 bit-widths (2.5, 3, 3.5, 4 bits); while this is explained by baseline cost, the resulting HV and "gap" metrics are not computed on a fully comparable basis and could bias comparisons in CoA-LoRA's favor.

The abstract's claim of "no additional time cost" is an overstatement given that CoA-LoRA still requires substantial training time (57-91 minutes) comparable to a single dedicated Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA run, plus additional overhead for the Pareto-based configuration search (GP fitting, finite-difference iterations) that is not clearly broken down in the time comparisons.

The total computational cost of the cyclic training procedure (Algorithm 1), including the cost of evaluating f1(C) on calibration data at each finite-difference step across potentially many layers/configurations, is not clearly quantified, making it hard to judge scalability to even larger models or larger configuration spaces.

Related work coverage of alternative dynamic/hypernetwork-based adapter generation methods (beyond quantization-specific LoRA variants) is limited, making it harder to contextualize the true novelty of the configuration-aware mapping approach.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation (e.g., configuration embeddings, segmented Pareto fronts) that could be streamlined; some details (e.g., exact procedure for translating continuous embedding updates into discrete configuration changes) are left underspecified even in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: efficiently adapting quantized LLMs with LoRA across heterogeneous device configurations without repeated fine-tuning per configuration.

The core idea of a lightweight configuration-aware hypernetwork that outputs small r×r adjustment matrices (rather than full LoRA matrices) is a reasonable and technically sound way to reduce output dimensionality while enabling per-layer adaptation.

The Pareto-based Gaussian process search combined with finite-difference guided coordinate optimization for selecting a high-quality training configuration set is a novel and non-trivial technical contribution to address the discrete, non-differentiable configuration search space.

Extensive experimental coverage across multiple model scales (RoBERTa-Large, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B/13B), multiple tasks (GLUE tasks, C4 perplexity, zero-shot downstream tasks), and multiple LoRA ranks (32/64/128), which supports some generality of the claims.
Useful ablations, including effect of configuration search vs. random extension, effect of number of Pareto segments U, and analysis of L1/L2 similarity motivating design choices (Appendix C.1).

Time-efficiency argument is compelling in principle: a single trained configuration-aware model amortizes the cost of per-configuration fine-tuning, which is demonstrated via reduced total training time relative to QLoRA/LQ-LoRA.
weaknesses: The reported accuracy gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal or negative across different ranks/tasks (e.g., Table 3 shows -0.63% and -3.13% gaps in some settings), which weakens the strength of the headline claim of '1.74%-8.89% gains' that appears to be selectively drawn from Table 2 rather than representative of the full body of results.

The primary competing baseline for 'no repeated fine-tuning' (Shared-LoRA) is a relatively weak strawman (a single adapter with no configuration awareness at all), making CoA-LoRA's advantage over it less informative; comparisons against more sophisticated elastic/flexible-bit-width baselines are missing.

The Hypervolume (HV) comparison in Table 2 may be unfair, since CoA-LoRA is evaluated over 50 configurations spanning 2.5-6.25 bits while QLoRA/LQ-LoRA are only evaluated at 5 discrete bit-widths, which could artificially inflate CoA-LoRA's HV due to denser support along the bit-width axis rather than intrinsically better per-point accuracy.

The overhead of the Pareto-based configuration search (GP fitting, finite-difference coordinate search over many iterations/configurations) is not clearly broken down separately from the configuration-aware model training time, making the 'no additional time cost' claim difficult to fully verify, especially as N (number of layers) grows into the hundreds for larger models.

The method's configuration representation and search space (Table 1) is tightly coupled to the NormalFloat (NF) quantization scheme; while an additional integer quantization experiment is provided, the core configuration-aware model and its 5-parameter layer representation are NF-specific, raising questions about generalization to other widely used non-uniform/outlier-aware quantization methods (e.g., AWQ, GPTQ-style saliency-based allocation) beyond simple RTN-style integer bit-widths.

Reproducibility is hindered by an apparently broken reference to the code repository ('Our implementation is available a' with no actual link), and the paper lacks variance/multiple-seed reporting for its accuracy numbers, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported (often small) improvements.

The generalization claim to 'unseen configurations' (Fig. 7) is only tested within the same average-bit-width range used during training/search (2.25-7.25 bits); extrapolation behavior outside this range, which is plausible in real heterogeneous-device deployment, is not evaluated.

The paper's presentation has some rough edges (e.g., unclear/incomplete sentences, dense notation overload with many symbols Q, C, f1, f2, z, m, b overloaded across sections), which somewhat hurts clarity and could be tightened.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: adapting LoRA to heterogeneous per-layer quantization configurations without repeated fine-tuning, which is meaningful for edge deployment.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental suite covering multiple models (RoBERTa-Large, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B/13B), multiple ranks, multiple bit budgets, and both NF and integer quantization formats.

Several ablations are provided (configuration search vs. random extension vs. frozen set, segment number U, unseen-configuration generalization, low-rank matrix similarity analysis) that at least partially support the design choices.

The idea of factorizing the adaptation into a lightweight per-layer r×r adjustment matrix rather than predicting full LoRA weights is a sensible way to control the output dimensionality of the hypernetwork.
weaknesses: A central and unexplained anomaly undermines the paper's core claims: a single shared configuration-aware model (CoA-LoRA) consistently outperforms QLoRA, which fine-tunes a dedicated adapter for each individual configuration (e.g., Table 3 shows CoA-LoRA beats QLoRA's per-configuration fine-tuning in 11/12 rank-task combinations, and Table 2 shows similar trends). It is highly counter-intuitive that a model amortized across dozens of configurations would systematically beat models specifically optimized for a single configuration; this raises concerns about whether baselines (QLoRA/LQ-LoRA) were fairly tuned (same epochs, learning rates, calibration data) or under-trained relative to CoA-LoRA, which is not adequately addressed in the paper.

The claim of 'no additional time cost' is overstated: the reported CoA-LoRA times (52-91 minutes) already dominate the entire training budget and do not clearly separate/include the cost of the Gaussian-process-based Pareto search, EHVI optimization, and iterative finite-difference coordinate search, which could be non-trivial as the number of layers/configurations grows; scalability of the search procedure itself is not analyzed.

Novelty is incremental: the paper mainly stitches together known components (a small hypernetwork/mapper conditioned on configuration embeddings, similar in spirit to prior LoRA-generation works cited in Sec 2.3; and Bayesian/Pareto multi-objective optimization for configuration selection) without a strong new theoretical or algorithmic contribution distinguishing it from this related line of work; no direct empirical comparison is made against ICM-LoRA, LoRA-Gen, or CONDP-DIFF despite discussing them as directly relevant.

Evaluation scope is narrow: experiments are limited to GLUE classification tasks and C4 perplexity/zero-shot accuracy on a handful of commonsense benchmarks; there is no evaluation on generative instruction-following, long-context, or chat-style tasks that are more representative of modern LLM deployment scenarios that motivate the paper (privacy-preserving edge LLM assistants).

No statistical robustness reporting (no multiple seeds, no variance/error bars) across any of the tables, making it hard to assess whether the (often small, e.g., 0.5-2%) reported gains are meaningful or within noise, especially given how close many HV/accuracy numbers are between methods.

The finite-difference gradient approximation over a discrete, non-differentiable, high-dimensional layer-embedding space (Eq. 7-8) is heuristic and its validity/convergence properties are not analyzed theoretically or empirically (e.g., sensitivity to step size δ beyond the fixed value of 1).

Several implementation and reproducibility details are thin or missing (e.g., GP kernel hyperparameters, calibration batch size sensitivity, exact stopping criteria for the alternating optimization in Algorithm 1, and how conflicts/duplicates in merged configuration sets are handled), which limits reproducibility despite an implementation link being mentioned but not detailed in the text.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: deploying quantized LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices with varying bit-width budgets without incurring the linear scaling cost of per-configuration LoRA fine-tuning.

The core design choice (mapping quantization configurations only to a lightweight r x r adjustment on L2, rather than the full LoRA parameter space) is motivated by an empirical observation (Appendix C.1/C.2) that adaptation-specific signal concentrates in L2, which is a reasonable and somewhat elegant way to make the mapping tractable.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple backbones (RoBERTa-Large, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B/13B), multiple GLUE tasks, multiple LoRA ranks (32/64/128), and both NormalFloat and integer mixed-precision quantization schemes.

Good set of ablations: effect of configuration search vs. random extension vs. frozen set, effect of number of Pareto segments U, seen vs. unseen configuration generalization, and zero-shot downstream task evaluation.

The reported efficiency gains (single ~1 hour training run covering 50 configurations vs. 20-40 minutes per configuration for one-to-one fine-tuning baselines) are a compelling practical advantage if the comparison is fair.
Reasonably detailed appendix with algorithmic pseudocode, architecture details, and parameter breakdowns that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing ideas (hypernetwork/config-conditioned parameter generation, Bayesian optimization with expected hypervolume improvement, finite-difference gradient approximation, Pareto filtering) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique.

Baselines are relatively dated (QLoRA 2023, LQ-LoRA 2024); more recent and directly relevant quantization-aware LoRA methods such as QA-LoRA (cited in related work but never empirically compared) are omitted, weakening the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claims.

The main comparison in Table 2 covers only 4-5 configurations for QLoRA/LQ-LoRA versus 50 for CoA-LoRA; while this favors demonstrating CoA-LoRA's amortization benefit, it also makes the head-to-head time/accuracy comparison somewhat asymmetric and could benefit from a controlled comparison at matched configuration counts.

No error bars or multi-seed variance reported; all results appear to be single-run, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported accuracy gains (some of which, e.g. MNLI r=64 gap of -0.63%, are quite small).

Evaluation is restricted to relatively small/older benchmarks (GLUE tasks and C4 perplexity); no evaluation on more modern or larger-scale LLM benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, instruction-following tasks) that would better demonstrate significance for current LLM deployment scenarios.

Several hyperparameters of the search procedure (finite-difference step size δ=1, number of iterations T2, choice of GP kernel) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness/generalization of the specific configuration search design.
Minor but notable presentation issues, e.g., an incomplete sentence 'Our implementation is available a' suggesting a broken/missing code link, which raises reproducibility concerns.

The overall pipeline (alternating configuration-aware model training, GP surrogate fitting, coordinate-wise finite-difference search, and segmented Pareto filtering) is fairly complex with many moving parts, which may hinder reproducibility and practical adoption without released code.
